newsitem.title: USA: Connecticut physicians cheer HMO reforms.
newsitem.headline: Connecticut physicians cheer HMO reforms.

text.p: Connecticut's decision to rein in the power of managed-care companies to deny treatment to their customers was cheered by physician and consumer groups on Thursday.
The state legislature voted Wednesday to give consumers new protections from tight-fisted medical insurers, including the right to overrule their health plan when denied coverage.

When patients who have been denied coverage exhaust the internal appeals of a health maintenance organization (HMO), they will be able to appeal to the Insurance Commissioner, who can overturn the health plan's decision.
Gov. John Rowland, a Repiublican, has said he will sign the bill, which is expected to become law on Oct 1.
The bill makes Connecticut only the second state in the U.S., after Rhode Island, to have a binding external appeals process.

Connecticut also joins 34 states in "bringing a measure of control to a health care system that threatened to leave crucial medical decisions in the hands of unqualified insurance bureaucrats," the Hartford Courant said in an editorial published Thursday.

"This is a big deal for Connecticut, because it's a recognition that...there's a need for some oversight for patient care that's provided by managed care organizations," said Mag Morelli, director of government relations for the Connecticut State Medical Society.
Morelli told Reuters that Connecticut could become a model for the rest of the U.S. because of the bill.
"It provides some checks and balances, and provides the patient the ability to get an independent medical review of their grievance or request for care," she said.

"The main significance is that consumers now have somewhere to go other than the HMOs to request a review. It used to be you could only go to the HMO to review it. Now at least you can go to the state."
About 1.4 million Connecticut residents are insured through some sort of managed care plan.

Morelli said the legislation represents a compromise, because the HMOs won on two major points -- that the state Insurance Department, and not the Department of Public Health, be the watchdog agency, and also that a proposed fee based on the number of health-plan subscribers be dropped.
